summary: Lolo NF lookout near Lolo Pass in Missoula County, MT: 1922 platform, cupola cabin, about 1934 L-4 tower around it, destroyed 1963; no source describes the site today.

facts.design: Region-1 log cupola cabin inside a 30-foot pole L-4 tower
facts.status_note: Destroyed in 1963 per firelookout.com and the library note on a 1957 photo; the Forest Fire Lookout Association index lists it as Tower Gone.

staffing.status: in use as a lookout station in 1928 per newspaper notices; later staffing not in the sources read

events.note: 30-foot pole platform built in 1922; the cupola cabin is dated to the 1920s (firelookout.com). A June 1922 newspaper item mentions a station recently built near Lolo Hot Springs.
1928 newspaper notices mention a man employed as a lookout at the Lolo Springs station and a Forest Service worker at Lolo Hot Springs who said he went weeks at a time without seeing anyone
30-foot pole L-4 tower built around the cupola cabin, about 1934 (firelookout.com)
Photo dated October 1957 shows a metal sign at the base of the lookout damaged by close-range shotgun blasts; a library note calls the lookout likely Lolo Springs

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Montana History Portal catalogue title names the Lolo Peak lookout, but its subject heading and library note name the Lolo Springs Lookout. The story follows the library note and says so.
The 1922 item says Lolo Hot Springs and the 1928 notice says Lolo Springs station. Both are treated as this lookout, which is likely but not stated by any source that names the station.

notes_for_editor: Platform (1922), L-4 tower (about 1934) and destruction (1963) agree between firelookout.com and the Montana History Portal library note. The 1928 staffing rests on two newspaper items that name no staff beyond the one notice; later staffing is not in the sources. The 1957 photo (Montana History Portal node 114482, UM Mansfield Library, photo FS99.05579, public domain per the record) is a good find, but the image URL was not captured, so no photos entry is included; add one if the image address is confirmed. Its catalogue title says Lolo Peak lookout. The FFLA Instagram post repeats the Lolo Springs identification but was not cited. Nothing in the sources describes what remains at the site or whether it is open to the public.
